rejected.title: Words and cultural context
card: The meaning of a word can depend on the culture of the people using it. The same word can mean different things in different communities.
Aboriginal English
This is a dialect of English spoken by many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. It has its own rules and ways of speaking. It is not incorrect English.
Country
To many Aboriginal people, Country means more than land. It includes the land, waters, plants, animals and stories a person belongs to, and has a duty to care for.
Mob
In Aboriginal English, mob can mean a group of people with a shared connection, such as family or community. It is often tied to a place.
rejected.remember: A word can carry meanings tied to a culture, so a reader should not assume it means only what they know.

a.q: An Aboriginal writer uses the word Country in a poem. Which reading best fits how many Aboriginal people use the word?
opts: A living place of land, waters, family and stories
A nation with its own government and flag
Any area of farmland away from a city
A single piece of land that a person owns
a.why: Country is tied to land, waters, stories and community, and to a person's duty to care for it. Reading it as owned land is tempting, but it misses the sense of belonging and responsibility.
a.clue: Think about belonging and care, not owning.

b.q: In a story, Kayla says, "My mob is coming to the footy on Saturday." Who is she most likely talking about?
opts: Her family and community
A crowd of angry strangers
Her school sports team only
Animals on her farm
b.why: In Aboriginal English, mob can mean a group with a shared connection, such as family or community. Reading it as a crowd of strangers uses the everyday meaning of mob and ignores the cultural one.
b.clue: Mob is about people connected to each other.

version.title: Words and cultural context
card: The meaning of a word can depend on the culture of the people using it. A reader who knows only one meaning may miss what a writer intends.
Aboriginal English
a dialect of English spoken by many Aboriginal people across Australia. Like every dialect, it is a form of English with its own consistent rules for sounds, grammar and meanings.
Country
for many Aboriginal people, Country means the land, waters, sky and living things a person belongs to, joined to them by family, stories and a duty of care.
Mob
in Aboriginal English, mob often means a person's family, kin or community. Asking "Who's your mob?" asks where and to whom someone belongs.
version.remember: Some words carry meanings from a culture, so read them in the context of the people who use them.

a.q: Why is Aboriginal English called a dialect rather than incorrect English?
opts: It follows its own rules, as every dialect does
It uses no words found in standard English
It is a separate language with no link to English
It is mostly written down rather than spoken
a.why: A dialect is a form of a language with its own consistent rules for sounds, grammar and meanings. Aboriginal English is a form of English, so it is not a separate language with no link to English.
a.clue: What does every dialect have, whoever speaks it?

b.q: In a story by an Aboriginal author, a character says she is visiting her mob on Country these holidays. What does she most likely mean?
opts: She is visiting family on the land she belongs to
She is visiting a crowd of people in the countryside
She is visiting her friends in another nation
She is visiting her relatives on land they have bought
b.why: Mob often means family, kin or community, and Country is the land a person belongs to. Reading mob as a crowd and Country as the countryside uses everyday meanings and misses the cultural ones.
b.clue: Read both words in the culture of the speaker.
